analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers and lets individuals import cheaper medicines.
analysis.headline: Introduced two weeks after the new Medicare drug law passed, the bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Medicare drug benefit law passed in late 2003. It would strike the provision that bars the government from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers, and it would allow individuals — not just pharmacists and wholesalers — to import prescription drugs, including from Canada. It would also repeal the Health Savings Accounts created by that law, remove private Medicare Advantage drug plans from the benefit, and require counterfeit-resistant packaging on prescription drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and other consumers who pay high prescription drug prices. Government price negotiation and legal personal importation of medicines from countries where drugs sell for less would put downward pressure on what seniors pay at the pharmacy. The counterfeit-packaging requirements would give consumers a visual way to verify a drug's authenticity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and other drug buyers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 'non-interference' clause of the 2003 Medicare drug law, which prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating prices with drug manufacturers or requiring a price structure for reimbursement, allowing direct government negotiation [S2][S3].

It lets 'qualifying individuals' who are neither pharmacists nor wholesalers import covered prescription drugs, replacing the 2003 law's Canada-importation provisions with a broader, permanent importation framework [S2][S3].

It repeals the Medicare Advantage Regional Plan Stabilization Fund, removes Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans from the qualifying drug plan definition, and repeals Health Savings Accounts, ending three channels of federal money and tax preference to private plans and accounts [S2][S3].

It makes drugs misbranded unless their packaging incorporates counterfeit-resistant technologies — visible features similar to those used on U.S. currency — so consumers can check authenticity with the naked eye [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices would face government negotiation and competition from lower-priced imported medicines. Private Medicare Advantage plans would lose a dedicated stabilization fund, and the financial industry would lose the Health Savings Account business created by the 2003 law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and private plans

drawbacks.text: The bill loosens importation safeguards: it repeals requirements that importers document the original source of products and provide information needed to protect public health, and it exempts many importers from authenticity and degradation testing, raising the risk that counterfeit or degraded drugs reach consumers [S2][S3].
Repealing Health Savings Accounts would eliminate a tax-advantaged savings vehicle that some consumers and employers had just gained under the 2003 law [S2][S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that government price negotiation and importation would cut into manufacturer revenue, which the industry argues funds research into new medicines; the bill offers no offsetting support for drug development.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are large and direct: seniors' drug costs under the new Medicare benefit were set to be substantial, and both negotiated prices and personal importation attack that cost from two directions. The main cost is the safety trade-off — the importation section strips away source documentation and testing requirements that the 2003 law's version of importation included, which is a genuine weakness even for supporters of importation. On balance the public gains outweigh that risk, but a more careful importation design would have kept stronger chain-of-custody rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died there when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle introduced the bill on November 25, 2003, days after the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act had been enacted, to revise that new law [S1][S2][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; no committee action, hearing, or floor vote is recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
Daschle gave introductory remarks on the bill twice, in November 2003 and again in May 2004, but the measure never advanced [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with the bill still in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the bar on government price negotiation, and Medicare Advantage plans kept the Regional Plan Stabilization Fund, because the bill never advanced. Consumers continued to pay the drug prices set under the 2003 law.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on it twice, in November 2003 and May 2004.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 25, 2003 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have repealed the industry's chief prize in the 2003 Medicare law — the bar on government price negotiation — which the industry had lobbied to include; the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats; the bill was referred to a Republican-chaired committee and received no Republican support or further action before the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the 'non-interference' clause that bars the government from negotiating drug prices, and would let individuals import cheaper medicines directly, opening their U.S. prices to competition from markets where the same drugs sell for less. Their interest in keeping the 2003 law intact runs against consumers' interest in lower prices.

The bill repeals the Regional Plan Stabilization Fund — federal money backstopping private regional plans — and removes Medicare Advantage drug plans from the qualifying plan definition. The fund is taxpayer money flowing to private plans; repealing it ends that channel.

industries.industry: Health savings and financial services industry
industries.note: Repealing Health Savings Accounts eliminates the tax-advantaged account business created by the 2003 law, a loss for financial firms but little direct cost to consumers beyond losing the option itself.
